questions.question: At whose London flat in September 1912 did Rupert Brooke, Wilfrid Gibson, John Drinkwater, and Harold Monro finalize the plan for the first 'Georgian Poetry' anthology?
options: Ezra Pound's flat at Church Walk, Kensington
Edward Marsh's chambers at Raymond Buildings, Gray's Inn
Robert Bridges's residence at Boars Hill, Oxford
Lady Ottoline Morrell's salon at Bedford Square
questions.explanation: On 19 September 1912 Brooke and Marsh met with Gibson Drinkwater Monro and Arundel del Re at Marsh Gray Inn chambers to launch Georgian Poetry.

questions.question: Which two poets were invited by Edward Marsh to appear in 'Georgian Poetry 1911–1912', but declined because one felt he belonged to an older era and the other refused his chosen poems?
options: Robert Frost and T. S. Eliot
Thomas Hardy and W. B. Yeats
Rudyard Kipling and Ford Madox Ford
A. E. Housman and Ezra Pound
questions.explanation: Housman modestly insisted he was not of the new generation while Ezra Pound declined when Marsh asked for two early poems instead of Ripostes.

questions.question: In the fourth (1919) and fifth (1922) volumes of 'Georgian Poetry', which two female poets were included by Edward Marsh for the very first time in the series?
options: Sylvia Townsend Warner and Ruth Pitter
questions.explanation: After three all-male volumes Marsh included four poems by Fredegond Shove in 1918-1919 and seven poems by Vita Sackville-West in 1920-1922.

questions.question: Although later associated with high modernism, which early passionate lyric by D. H. Lawrence was included by Edward Marsh in the inaugural 'Georgian Poetry 1911–1912'?
questions.explanation: Marsh included Lawrence Snap-Dragon in Georgian Poetry 1911-1912 alongside Service of All the Dead and Seven Seals in Later volumes.

questions.question: Which brief twenty-two-line speech from Isaac Rosenberg's verse play 'Moses' was the only piece by Rosenberg ever printed by Edward Marsh in 'Georgian Poetry 1916–1917'?
questions.explanation: Marsh printed only the short speech of the Young Hebrew beginning Ah Koelue from Rosenberg self-published 1916 play Moses.

questions.question: What was the title of the four-issue quarterly periodical published in 1914 from Lascelles Abercrombie's cottage in Dymock, which first printed Rupert Brooke's '1914' war sonnets?
questions.explanation: Abercrombie Gibson Drinkwater and Brooke published four issues of New Numbers from Ryton Dymock in 1914 printing The Soldier in its final issue.

questions.question: On what exact pre-war date in June 1914 did Edward Thomas's train make an unscheduled stop at Adlestrop station while he was traveling from London to visit Robert Frost?
questions.explanation: Thomas recorded the stop at Adlestrop in his notebook on 24 June 1914 while traveling from Paddington to Ledbury and wrote the poem in January 1915.

questions.question: Which famous poem by Robert Frost, collected in 'Mountain Interval' (1916), was originally written as a gentle teasing response to Edward Thomas's indecisiveness on their Dymock walks?
options: Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening
questions.explanation: Frost sent a draft of The Road Not Taken to Edward Thomas in 1915 mocking Thomas habit of regretting whichever forest path they had not chosen.

questions.question: How many annual 'cycles' of the modernist anthology 'Wheels' were edited by Edith Sitwell between 1916 and 1921 as an avant-garde rebellion against 'Georgian Poetry'?
questions.explanation: Edith Sitwell and her brothers Osbert and Sacheverell published six cycles of Wheels between December 1916 and 1921.

questions.question: Prior to Siegfried Sassoon's 1920 edition of Wilfred Owen's 'Poems', who dedicated the 1919 fourth cycle of 'Wheels' to Owen's memory and first printed seven of his war poems in book form?
questions.explanation: Edith Sitwell and Osbert Sitwell dedicated Wheels 1919 Fourth Cycle to Wilfred Owen and printed Strange Meeting Disabled and five other poems.

questions.question: Which conservative literary monthly, founded and edited by Sir John Collings Squire from November 1919 to 1934, became the organ of the neo-Georgian coterie dubbed the 'Squirearchy'?
questions.explanation: J C Squire launched The London Mercury in November 1919 championing traditional Georgian verse against Eliot Pound and the Sitwells.

questions.question: In his March 1918 review of 'Georgian Poetry 1916–1917' in 'The Egoist' ('Verse Pleasant and Unpleasant'), what chief defect did T. S. Eliot diagnose in the Georgian poets?
options: Their radical Marxist propaganda in rural ballads
Their insular provincialism and reliance on trivial 'pleasantness'
Their pedantic obsession with classical Greek and Latin epigraphs
Their excessive imitation of French Symbolist free verse
questions.explanation: Eliot criticized the Georgians for caressing everything they touched into a complacent provincial pleasantness of rainbows cuckoos and daffodils.

questions.question: In his December 1919 essay in 'The Athenaeum' reviewing 'Georgian Poetry 1918–1919', how did John Middleton Murry characterize the later Georgian school?
options: As a decadent offshoot of the 1890s Rhymers' Club
As a bold return to Metaphysical wit and paradox
As an austere revival of Anglo-Saxon alliterative meter
questions.explanation: Murry condemned the right wing of the Georgian coalition for false simplicity and a complacent cult of nature without tragic conviction.

questions.question: Which 1931 satirical poem in heroic couplets by the South African poet Roy Campbell fiercely lampooned the London neo-Georgian literary establishment and Bloomsbury?
questions.explanation: Modeled on Pope Dunciad Roy Campbell The Georgiad 1931 mocked J C Squire Vita Sackville-West and the Georgian pastoralists.

questions.question: Which gritty 1911 narrative poem in octosyllabic couplets by John Masefield—published in 'The English Review'—depicts the drunken poacher Saul Kane's spiritual conversion?
options: The Widow in the Bye Street
questions.explanation: Printed by Austin Harrison in The English Review in October 1911 The Everlasting Mercy electrified readers with its raw colloquial realism.

questions.question: Which 1921 novel by Walter de la Mare—winner of the James Tait Black Memorial Prize—portrays the inner life of a cultured Victorian woman Miss M., who stands barely three feet tall?
questions.explanation: Walter de la Mare published Memoirs of a Midget in 1921 exploring beauty alienation and scale through the diminutive heroine Miss M.

questions.question: Which prominent playwright and critic received a self-published copy of 'The Soul's Destroyer' mailed from a London doss-house by W. H. Davies in 1905 and helped launch his career?
questions.explanation: Impressed by the fresh talent in The Soul Destroyer Shaw sent Davies money recommended him to critics and later wrote the preface to Super-Tramp.

questions.question: Under what title was Siegfried Sassoon's July 1917 statement against the continuation of World War I read in the House of Commons and printed in 'The Times'?
options: Finished with the War: A Soldier's Declaration
No More Parades: A Officer's Manifesto
A Protest from the Western Front
An Open Letter to the War Office
questions.explanation: Drafted with help from Bertrand Russell and Middleton Murry Sassoon declaration was read in Parliament by Hastings Lees-Smith on 30 July 1917.

questions.question: Which pioneering neurologist, anthropologist, and army psychiatrist treated Siegfried Sassoon at Craiglockhart War Hospital in 1917?
questions.explanation: Captain W H R Rivers treated Sassoon with humane talking therapy at Craiglockhart and became a father figure to him until Rivers death in 1922.

questions.question: What was the title of the Craiglockhart War Hospital fortnightly magazine edited by Wilfred Owen in 1917, in which Owen published his first war poems?
questions.explanation: Named after the many-headed monster because patients lived in the former Hydropathic establishment The Hydra was edited by Owen in 1917.

questions.question: Before crossing out her name on the manuscript, to which popular patriotic writer of recruitment verses ('Who's for the Game?') did Wilfred Owen ironically dedicate drafts of 'Dulce et Decorum Est'?
questions.explanation: Owen initially dedicated Dulce et Decorum Est To Jessie Pope etc and To a certain Poetess before removing the name to universalize the address My friend.

questions.question: Which twenty-year-old Scottish poet, killed by a sniper at the Battle of Loos in October 1915, wrote the stark sonnet beginning 'When you see millions of the mouthless dead'?
questions.explanation: Found in his kitbag after his death at Loos and published in Marlborough and Other Poems 1916 Sorley sonnet rejected sentimental consolation.

questions.question: Which aristocratic cavalry officer wrote the ecstatic 1915 combat lyric 'Into Battle' ('The naked earth is warm with spring'), printed in 'The Times' on the day his death was announced?
questions.explanation: Captain Julian Grenfell of the Royal Dragoons wrote Into Battle in April 1915 and died of a shell splinter to the head at Boulogne in May 1915.

questions.question: Which Gloucestershire poet and composer, gassed at Passchendaele in 1917, published the wartime verse collections 'Severn and Somme' (1917) and 'War's Embers' (1919)?
questions.explanation: Ivor Gurney set Housman and Edward Thomas to music and wrote poignant poems of Gloucestershire and the trenches before his 1922 asylum confinement.

questions.question: Which of the following gives the exact chronological sequence of the four novels that constitute Ford Madox Ford's tetralogy 'Parade's End' (1924–1928)?
options: The Good Soldier, Some Do Not..., No More Parades, and The Last Post
Some Do Not..., No More Parades, A Man Could Stand Up—, and The Last Post
A Man Could Stand Up—, Some Do Not..., No More Parades, and Armistice Day
No More Parades, Some Do Not..., The Last Post, and A Man Could Stand Up—
questions.explanation: Ford published Some Do Not in 1924 No More Parades in 1925 A Man Could Stand Up in 1926 and The Last Post in 1928.

questions.question: What original title had Ford Madox Ford chosen for 'The Good Soldier' before publisher John Lane objected in 1915 that a gloomy title would hurt wartime sales?
questions.explanation: Opening extracts appeared in Wyndham Lewis Blast in 1914 under the title The Saddest Story before Ford sarcastically suggested The Good Soldier.

questions.question: In E. M. Forster's 'Howards End' (1910), which three families represent cultured Anglo-German liberal idealism, pragmatic imperial capitalism, and struggling lower-middle-class clerkdom?
options: The Schlegels, the Wilcoxes, and the Basts
The Pembrokes, the Ansells, and the Wonhams
The Herritons, the Abbotts, and the Carellas
The Honeychurches, the Emersons, and the Vyses
questions.explanation: Margaret and Helen Schlegel embody culture Henry Wilcox and his children embody business power and Leonard and Jacky Bast embody poor clerkdom.

questions.question: Which novel did E. M. Forster write in 1913–1914 after visiting Edward Carpenter, insisting that it end happily in the 'greenwood' and remain unpublished until after his death?
questions.explanation: Dedicated To a Happier Year Forster novel Maurice unites Maurice Hall and the gamekeeper Alec Scudder and was published posthumously in 1971.

questions.question: What are the exact titles of the three structural divisions of E. M. Forster's 1924 novel 'A Passage to India'?
options: Part I: Islam, Part II: Nothingness, and Part III: Hinduism
Part I: Winter, Part II: Monochrome, and Part III: Monsoon
Part I: Mosque, Part II: Caves, and Part III: Temple
Part I: Chandrapore, Part II: Marabar, and Part III: Mau
questions.explanation: Forster divided A Passage to India into Mosque Caves and Temple aligning with the cool weather the hot weather and the rains.

questions.question: Which eccentric, mystical Hindu professor of Chandrapore College sings a song to Krishna at Fielding's tea party and presides over the festival in Part III of 'A Passage to India'?
questions.explanation: Professor Narayan Godbole Deccani Brahman embodies Hindu pantheistic inclusiveness during the birth ceremony of Lord Krishna at Mau.

questions.question: Across which three generations of the Brangwen family in the Erewash Valley does D. H. Lawrence's 'The Rainbow' (1915) unfold?
options: Alfred and Gertrude; Paul and Miriam; and William Morel
Thomas and Crich; Gerald and Gudrun; and Rupert Birkin
Tom and Lydia Lensky; Will and Anna; and Ursula Brangwen
Aaron Sisson; Lilly; and Kate Leslie
questions.explanation: The Rainbow traces farmer Tom Brangwen marriage to the Polish widow Lydia Lensky their stepdaughter Anna marriage to Will and Ursula quest for freedom.

questions.question: At the climax of D. H. Lawrence's 'Women in Love' (1920), how does the industrialist mine-owner Gerald Crich meet his death in the Tyrolean Alps?
options: He wanders alone up into the snowbound mountains and freezes to death near a half-buried crucifix
He is killed in a duel with the German sculptor Loerke
He leaps from a mountain cable-car after Gudrun rejects him
He drowns beneath the ice of a frozen Alpine lake
questions.explanation: After nearly strangling Gudrun and striking Loerke Gerald Crich skis upward into an icy cul-de-sac in the Alps and freezes to death.

questions.question: What are the exact titles of the three parts of Virginia Woolf's 1927 novel 'To the Lighthouse'?
options: Part I: The Window, Part II: Time Passes, and Part III: The Lighthouse
Part I: The Island, Part II: The Great War, and Part III: The Voyage
Part I: Evening, Part II: Night, and Part III: Morning
Part I: Mrs. Ramsay, Part II: Darkness, and Part III: Lily's Canvas
questions.explanation: To the Lighthouse is structured in an H-shape with two single days The Window and The Lighthouse bridged by the ten-year corridor Time Passes.

questions.question: Who are the six characters whose interwoven soliloquies trace their lives around the silent, absent hero Percival in Virginia Woolf's 'The Waves' (1931)?
options: Bernard, Susan, Rhoda, Neville, Jinny, and Louis
Eleanor, Delia, Morris, Martin, Rose, and Peggy
Clarissa, Peter, Sally, Richard, Septimus, and Lucrezia
Jacob, Bonamy, Clara, Florinda, Fanny, and Sandra
questions.explanation: Three men Bernard Neville and Louis and three women Susan Jinny and Rhoda speak in dramatic soliloquies framed by nine italicized coastal interludes.

questions.question: In the Gilbert and Linati schemas for James Joyce's 'Ulysses' (1922), what are the Homeric titles of Episode 1 (at the Martello Tower) and Episode 18 (Molly Bloom's monologue)?
questions.explanation: Ulysses opens at 8 a.m. with Episode 1 Telemachus featuring Stephen Dedalus and Buck Mulligan and ends with Episode 18 Penelope spoken by Molly Bloom.

questions.question: Which longest, hallucination-filled fifteenth episode of James Joyce's 'Ulysses' is formatted entirely as a surreal stage play set in Dublin's 'Nighttown' brothel district?
questions.explanation: Episode 15 Circe takes place at midnight in Bella Cohen brothel in Nighttown where Leopold Bloom and Stephen Dedalus confront their deepest unconscious guilt.

questions.question: From which first-century Latin work by Petronius did T. S. Eliot take the Greek-and-Latin epigraph to 'The Waste Land' (1922), in which the Cumaean Sibyl says 'I want to die'?
questions.explanation: After Pound dissuaded Eliot from using an epigraph from Conrad Heart of Darkness Eliot chose Trimalchio speech on the Sibyl from Petronius Satyricon.

questions.question: In Part III ('The Fire Sermon') of 'The Waste Land', which blind mythological figure—called in Eliot's notes 'the most important personage in the poem'—witnesses the typist's seduction?
questions.explanation: Eliot note to line 218 states that what Tiresias sees in fact is the substance of the poem uniting both sexes in his blind foresuffering consciousness.

questions.question: In Part II of T. S. Eliot's 1935 verse drama 'Murder in the Cathedral', how do the Four Knights startle the audience immediately after slaying Archbishop Thomas Becket?
options: They chant the Latin Penitential Psalms together with the Women of Canterbury
They remove their helmets to reveal that they are identical to the Four Tempters in masks
They perform a silent medieval dumb-show depicting the coronation of Henry II
They step forward and address the audience in modern political prose to justify the murder
questions.explanation: Breaking the twelfth-century verse frame Reginald Fitz Urse and the knights deliver slick modern platform speeches asking the audience to excuse their rational act.

questions.question: Which 1916 one-act play by W. B. Yeats—first performed in Lady Cunard's London drawing room with masks by Edmund Dulac—inaugurated Yeats's adaptation of Japanese Noh drama?
questions.explanation: Prompted by Ezra Pound work on Ernest Fenollosa Noh manuscripts Yeats staged At the Hawk Well in April 1916 with Michio Ito dancing the Guardian of the Well.

questions.question: Why did nationalist demonstrators riot at Dublin's Abbey Theatre during the fourth performance of Sean O'Casey's 'The Plough and the Stars' in February 1926?
options: Because the play portrayed Michael Collins signing the partition treaty in London
Because Act II brought the Irish flags into a public house alongside the prostitute Rosie Redmond
Because Yeats invited the British Viceroy to sit in the front row on opening night
Because the play mocked Catholic priests refusing absolution to Easter Rising rebels
questions.explanation: Protesters led by Hannah Sheehy-Skeffington stormed the Abbey stage over the pub scene in Act II prompting Yeats famous rebuke You have disgraced yourselves again.

questions.question: In R. C. Sherriff's 1928 war drama 'Journey's End', set in a dugout before St. Quentin in March 1918, who is the whiskey-dependent company commander idolized by young Jimmy Raleigh?
questions.explanation: First played by a young Laurence Olivier in December 1928 Captain Dennis Stanhope masks his three years of trench nerve strain with whiskey.

questions.question: Which four nineteenth-century figures are the biographical subjects of Lytton Strachey's landmark 1918 iconoclastic study 'Eminent Victorians'?
options: Queen Victoria, Prince Albert, Lord Melbourne, and Benjamin Disraeli
William Gladstone, Lord Palmerston, Cardinal Newman, and Charles Darwin
Cardinal Manning, Florence Nightingale, Dr. Thomas Arnold, and General Gordon
Thomas Carlyle, John Ruskin, Matthew Arnold, and Lord Macaulay
questions.explanation: Strachey dissected Victorian religion humanitarianism education and imperialism through Manning Nightingale Arnold of Rugby and General Gordon.

questions.question: In what futuristic calendar year—measured from the production of Henry Ford's Model T—does Aldous Huxley's 'Brave New World' (1932) open, and who is the World Controller for Western Europe?
options: A.F. 632, under Resident World Controller Mustapha Mond
A.F. 500, under World Controller Helmholtz Watson
A.F. 1984, under World Controller Bernard Marx
questions.explanation: Set in this year of stability A.F. 632 After Ford Brave New World features Mustapha Mond one of the ten World Controllers.

questions.question: Which character in Aldous Huxley's 'Brave New World' (1932)—raised on the New Mexico Reservation reading Shakespeare—quotes Miranda's words from 'The Tempest' before hanging himself?
questions.explanation: Born naturally to Linda on the Malpais Reservation John the Savage initially greets the World State with O brave new world before retreating to a Surrey lighthouse.

questions.question: Who is the lonely timber merchant with a dark birthmark on his cheek who champions Dr. Veraswami before shooting himself in George Orwell's 1934 debut novel 'Burmese Days'?
questions.explanation: Drawing on his five years in the Indian Imperial Police in Burma Orwell portrayed John Flory disgraced at church by his Burmese mistress Ma Hla May.

questions.question: Which aspiring poet in George Orwell's 1936 novel 'Keep the Aspidistra Flying' wages a one-man war on the 'money-god' before returning to an advertising firm when Rosemary becomes pregnant?
questions.explanation: Gordon Comstock quits the New Albion publicity firm to work in a cheap bookshop and write his poem London Pleasures before buying an aspidistra for his flat.

questions.question: Which 1935 satirical play co-authored by W. H. Auden and Christopher Isherwood follows Alan Norman across Europe searching for Sir Francis Crewe, who has accompanied him disguised as a dog?
questions.explanation: Produced by Rupert Doone Group Theatre in January 1936 The Dog Beneath the Skin or Where is Francis satirized fascism and British village complacency.

questions.question: Which of the following statements concerning the Georgian Period (1910–1936) is NOT correct?
options: John Galsworthy received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1932
Edward Marsh edited five volumes of 'Georgian Poetry' between 1912 and 1922
John Masefield was appointed Poet Laureate in 1930 following the death of Robert Bridges
D. H. Lawrence was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1928 for 'Lady Chatterley's Lover'
questions.explanation: D H Lawrence never received the Nobel Prize and Lady Chatterley Lover was privately printed in Florence in 1928 and banned in Britain.

questions.question: Which of the following character-and-work pairings from the Georgian Period (1910–1936) is NOT correctly matched?
options: Christopher Tietjens — John Galsworthy's 'The Forsyte Saga'
Paul Pennyfeather — Evelyn Waugh's 'Decline and Fall'
Philip Carey — W. Somerset Maugham's 'Of Human Bondage'
Lily Briscoe — Virginia Woolf's 'To the Lighthouse'
questions.explanation: Christopher Tietjens is the central hero of Ford Madox Ford tetralogy Parade End whereas Soames Forsyte is the central character of The Forsyte Saga.
